item.title: Data Pyramid for Embodied Manipulation: A Survey
item.description:
Relevance: 46% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yifan Ye, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lv, Bohan Hou, Jun Cen, Lingdong Kong, Duo Zheng, Tianxing Chen, Jiaming Liu, Ziang Cao, Yunfan Lou, Wei Chow, Xian Sun, Yingshuo Wang, Kuangzhi Ge, Xiaowei Chi, Xidong Zhang, Zhibo Pang, Yiwu Zhong, Sirui Han, Zhihe Lu, Weihao Yuan, Qifeng Chen, Michael Yu Wang, Yao Mu, Ziwei Liu, Jianfei Yang, Ping Luo, Shanghang Zhang
arXiv:2607.24744v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal foundation models learned to see and to speak by consuming the whole internet. Embodied agents admit no such shortcut, since they require data that couple observations with physical states and actions. These signals can be provided, to varying degrees, by multiple data sources. In this work, we organize the embodied data ecosystem as a "pyramid'' spanning five complementary sources: real-robot data, UMI-style data, egocentric and exocentric data, simulation data, and general vision-language data. We organize the pyramid around the tension between scalability and robot alignment, and further characterize each source in terms of data quality, diversity, reusability, and physical fidelity. We then analyze recent embodied foundation models through the lens of data recipes, examining how different sources are selected, aligned, and mixed during pretraining. For embodied brain models, vision-language-action models, and world-action models alike, we relate data composition to capabilities in perception, reasoning, planning, action generation, and world prediction. To facilitate community use, we additionally consolidate over 10,000 hours of trajectories from widely used robot datasets into a unified LeRobot format, with transparent frame-level quality annotations for filtering. We close by discussing six open challenges: building large-scale tactile datasets, collecting failure and recovery data, developing scalable data-collection pipelines, aligning actions across embodiments, leveraging egocentric data for dexterous manipulation, and designing principled data recipes for robot learning. We hope this work lays the foundation for the design of next-generation embodied systems.

item.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
item.description:
Relevance: 42% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren
arXiv:2611.18397v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

item.title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 40% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang, Jinqiao Wang
arXiv:2611.22415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

item.title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
item.description:
Relevance: 38% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Haojun Tang, Wenda Zhao, Xiang Zhou, Qiwei Lin, Lida Huang, Yan Wang
arXiv:2611.15481v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

item.title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
item.description:
Relevance: 38% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Guoqing Wang, Pin Tang, Xiangxuan Ren, Chao Ma
arXiv:2611.22880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

item.title: SpikWM: Efficient End-to-End Spiking World Modeling for Visual Planning
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shuhan Ye, Hongbin Yu, Chong Wang, Hui Lu, Jiaming He, Yi Yu, Jiangbo Qian, Xudong Jiang
arXiv:2611.22981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.

item.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Emilio Ferrara
arXiv:2611.20385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 75% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 40%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 80-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

item.title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Sheng Lu, Guangpin Tao, Tong Lu, Ying Tai
arXiv:2611.21812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.

item.title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ting-Hsuan Chen, Siheng Zhao, Han Jiang, Qi Pan, Louison Lu, Jiaheng Luo, Henghui Bao, Yiyu Chen, Quan Nguyen, Yue Wang
arXiv:2611.22275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

item.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuhao Lu, Jiongxu Chen, Hexiang Wei, Jiajin Wu, Juelin Li, Mingjian Liang, Fan Yang, Zhuowei Liang, Zihao Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Lin Shao
arXiv:2610.39278v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.

item.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Tian Lyu, Yichen Jiang, Ziyuan Cheng, Yunda Yan, Xiangyu Pan, Junjie Jiang, Jialin Yu, Boyu Ning, Pietro Li\`o, Fan Mo
arXiv:2611.22543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

item.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Weiguang Zhao, Yifan Wang, Ni Yang, Yating Wang, Xingyu Miao, Yankai Jiang, Mulin Yu, Tao Lu, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
arXiv:2611.23140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

item.title: ReactWorld: Structuring Interaction Responses for Embodied Video Generation
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Hanwei Liu, Huijia Zhang, Hanzhang Wang, Guangyu Liu, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang
arXiv:2611.06120v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.

item.title: Exploration stabilizes learning dynamics and promotes cooperation in stochastic games
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Yuxin Geng, Xingru Chen, Wolfram Barfuss, Longzhao Liu, Xin Wang, Shaoting Tang, Feng Fu
arXiv:2601.07142v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding and stabilizing collective learning dynamics is a central challenge in stochastic games. Although exploration is widely used in learning algorithms, its effects on the coupled dynamics of agents and their environment remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we derive analytical equations for entropy-regularized actor-critic learning in stochastic games by separating the timescales of value estimation and policy adaptation. Without exploration, the system preserves a weighted volume in the policy phase space, ruling out asymptotically stable fully mixed equilibria. We provide a unified characterization of exploration's effects on objective curvature, preference dynamics in log-ratio coordinates, and the forgetting of past action preferences. Exploration reduces local volume expansion and can stabilize learning dynamics. In a two-state Matching Pennies game, it suppresses chaotic learning and promotes convergence to a mixed equilibrium. In a Prisoner's Dilemma with environmental feedback, intermediate exploration eliminates the defective attractor and expands the basin of attraction of the cooperative equilibrium. Our findings reveal how exploration shapes collective behavior, informing the design of cooperative and resilient multi-agent systems.

item.title: CascadeJEPA: Enhancing 3D Geometric Representations via Spatially Coupled Cascaded Prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Kailai Zhou, Ziqi Chen, Xiaoning Xu, Yuefeng Wu, Zixuan Fu, Zijun Lin, Zhihao Li, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Xun Cao, Bihan Wen
arXiv:2611.22686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.

item.title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Amish Sethi, Boya Zeng, Wenhao Chai, Zhuang Liu
arXiv:2611.22427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: https://github.com/AmishSethi/visual-generative-lab.

item.title: Intra-Agent Motion and Inter-Agent Relation Learning for Map-Free Trajectory Prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Wenyi Xiong, Jian Chen, Wenhua Chen, Ziheng Qi
arXiv:2512.02368v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trajectory prediction is essential for safe planning and decision-making in autonomous driving. Map-free prediction improves deployment flexibility by removing the dependence on high-definition maps, but it also loses explicit road-topology and lane-connectivity priors. Consequently, the model must recover stable motion cues from short histories while resolving prospective interaction relations without lane-level guidance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a map-free trajectory prediction framework centered on a novel Goal-Conditioned Expert-Routed Transformer (GCERT). A lightweight intra-agent front-end first decomposes projected historical motion features into a smooth trend and a local detail residual through a centered moving average. Component-specific residual projections transform the two signals before a causal temporal Transformer summarizes their recombined evolution. GCERT employs dual-level expert routing: edge-level relation experts generate interaction-specific messages, while node-level state experts adapt the transformation after message aggregation. Predicted motion goals update the node representations and construct prospective relative-geometry and orientation edge features before the final interaction layer, thereby conditioning attention, relation-specific message generation, and state transformation. GCERT therefore determines not only which neighboring agents should be attended to, but also what relation-specific information should be transmitted and how the aggregated node state should be transformed. The resulting representations are decoded into multimodal future trajectories and jointly optimized with trajectory-regression, mode-classification, and goal-prediction objectives.

item.title: Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Gabriel Sarch, Declan Campbell, Nicholas Budny, Kia Ghods, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Jonathan D. Cohen, Brenden M. Lake, Taylor W. Webb
arXiv:2611.23209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.

item.title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Hiroshi Higashi
arXiv:2611.22440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

item.title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Nguyen Quang Trung, Hoang Phan, Shuo Sun, Longyin Zhang, AiTi Aw
arXiv:2611.23034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.

item.title: Pixel is All You Need
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jie Chu, Haoting Shi, Fucheng Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Junwei Liao, Ying Wen, Muning Wen
arXiv:2611.22820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

item.title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Tianci Xie, Li Chen, Pinxue Guo, Rui Zheng
arXiv:2611.22790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.

item.title: Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Renaud Lambiotte
arXiv:2611.04886v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills needed for future work. We consider a population of agents who perform a task either with their own skill or with the help of AI. Agents tend to imitate more successful peers, and their skills evolve in time: improving with practice and eroding with reliance on AI. We study, analytically and with simulations, the collective consequences of AI adoption. We show that the mechanism of skill erosion makes adoption bistable and that the long-term behaviour of the population depends on how skills are distributed: populations with the same adoption and mean skill can reach opposite asymptotic states, depending on how expertise is shared between AI users and non-users. A deterministic description that follows the mean skills of the two groups and the variance of skills among non-users predicts the outcome of individual runs as accurately as the simulations allow, whereas the means alone are not sufficient. We also consider the situation when the benefit of AI improves in time. In that case, adoption can jump abruptly, and a temporary increase in benefit, such as in a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its original value. Skill erosion therefore creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

item.title: Building verifiable databases at scale from the chemical literature via a multi-agent system
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yufan Chen, Ching Ting Leung, Bowen Yu, Haifan Zhou, Jianwei Sun, Yong Huang, Linyan Li, Hao Chen, Hanyu Gao
arXiv:2507.20230v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accelerating chemical research with artificial intelligence requires high-quality databases. However, many reactions exist only as graphics drawn for human readers, which machines must read exactly. Specialist software is precise but rigid, whereas multimodal language models are flexible yet often write incorrect structures; neither flags errors. We present ChemEAGLE, a multi-agent system where tools supply structures and a language model extends their reach through judgments that programs apply. On 424 published graphics, its F1 score for exactly correct reactions was 82.2%, against 47.7% for a tool-equipped generalist agent, and calibrated confidence limited review to 35% of reactions at 96.6% accuracy. Without review, it built a 60,103-reaction photochemistry database whose records trained models to rank conditions and predict products. Verifiable databases can thus be built at scale.

item.title: DualTopo: Spatio-Temporal Lane Graph Generation with Dual Latent World Models and Parallel Query Supervision
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yiming Yang, Hongbin Lin, Yueru Luo, Suzhong Fu, Chao Zheng, Xinrui Yan, Kun Tang, Chen Lv, Shuguang Cui, Zhen Li
arXiv:2507.23325v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lane topology reasoning constructs a spatiotemporal road graph G = (V, E) in bird's-eye view (BEV), providing structured road representations for planning-oriented autonomous driving. Stream-based methods propagate temporal cues at both the query and BEV levels, yet suffer from two critical limitations: (1) initialized queries receive insufficient supervision, as temporal queries dominate Hungarian matching and leave them undertrained; and (2) temporal propagation is weakened by BEV boundary information loss during feature warping. Since initialized queries serve as propagation anchors, particularly at the first frame, these deficiencies compound across frames and degrade graph generation quality. We propose DualTopo, a spatio-temporal lane graph generation framework with dual latent world models and dual parallel decoder pathways. The dual-pathway decoder supervises temporal and initialized queries concurrently, ensuring initialized queries are well-trained and serve as reliable anchors. Dual latent world models conditioned on ego-motion propagate latent state representations from past observations to the present, substantially improving spatiotemporal graph generation. Extensive experiments on OpenLane-V2 demonstrate leading lane detection accuracy and competitive topology graph prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/YimingYang23/DualTopo.

item.title: Teaching What to Look For: Privileged Perception Questions for Agentic On-Policy Distillation in Video Captioning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yifan Xu, Ruopeng Gao, Zhixiao Wang, Jiafu Tang, Yichun Yang, Zihao Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Limin Wang
arXiv:2611.22755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detailed video captioning requires comprehensive and faithful descriptions of objects, actions, and temporal events. Fixed-frame sampling, however, can miss brief motions, small objects, and other fine-grained evidence, motivating captioning agents that actively seek relevant moments and inspect local regions. Training such behavior is challenging because, unlike video question answering, generic captioning instructions do not specify what visual evidence should be acquired. We propose Perception-Question On-Policy Distillation (PQ-OPD), which uses training-only Perception Questions (PQs) to guide active video perception. PQs specify what should be inspected without revealing the corresponding answers, encouraging the teacher to explore the video more comprehensively and focus on relevant visual evidence. Along trajectories generated by the student, on-policy distillation transfers this guidance to the student's reasoning, tool calls, and captions; no PQs are required at inference. Across three detailed-captioning and two caption-to-QA benchmarks, PQ-OPD consistently improves the corresponding untrained agents across teacher-student scales and input-frame budgets. Under our evaluation protocol, PQ-OPD achieves the strongest primary-metric results among the compared open-source models on DREAM-1K, CaReBench, ShortVidBench, MotionBench, and VidCapBench-AE. Our ablations, together with analysis of temporal coverage and answer leakage, further indicates that the student internalizes the training-time guidance as a more effective video exploration policy.

item.title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Nikhil J. Dhinagar, Rishab Pendam, Harmony S. Cen, Sophia I. Thomopoulos, John P. John, Mahir H. Khan, Sook-Lei Liew, Erik Kaestner, Carrie McDonald, Paul M. Thompson
arXiv:2611.21955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($\epsilon$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

item.title: Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
arXiv:2611.22351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

item.title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Do Xuan Long, Long T. Le, Yiwen Song, Min-Yen Kan, Tomas Pfister, Yale Song
arXiv:2611.22673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

item.title: RiDEx: Reward-Informed Directional Exploration for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Song Yan, Chenfeng Wang, Wei Zhai, Xingchen Wang, Tao Zhang, Yawen Shao, Shi Pan, Min Li, Zheng-Jun Zha
arXiv:2611.22052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. While existing approaches improve sampling and policy optimization, they still rely largely on isotropic random perturbations in a high-dimensional latent space for exploration. Such variation often spends the perturbation budget on changes with little influence on the target reward, making exploration inefficient. We study where diffusion models should explore and how to learn from that exploration. We introduce Reward-Informed Directional Exploration (RiDEx), which concentrates local exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field. Conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients propose the subspace, and equal-and-opposite perturbations at the same generation state measure its terminal reward response. The reward difference supplies signed local supervision in the explored coordinates, while all generated images contribute to global DiffusionNFT learning. RiDEx thereby couples exploration-space selection with feedback about the changes it produces. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, RiDEx attains the highest peak rewards among the evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks. Its gradient-direction instantiation achieves 15x and 29x target-attainment speedups over DiffusionNFT on HPSv2 and PickScore, measured in H200 GPU hours. Controlled experiments confirm that reward-aligned directions elicit stronger responses at equal perturbation magnitude, and that applying their measured credit improves curve-average reward across all four tasks.

item.title: Transient Signal Propagation in Heterogeneous Networks under Various Inputs
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Xiaoge Bao, Wei P. Dai, Jan Nagler, Wei Lin
arXiv:2510.19481v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transient signals in neural, biological and technological networks rarely follow a single route. Their strength and timing depend on where the input enters, on the intrinsic dynamics of each node visited, and on the feedforward and recurrent pathways that carry it. Previous theory has clarified important limits of signal propagation, but often for a single input type, averaged network structure, or asymptotic regimes. It has remained unclear how finite heterogeneous networks transform sustained, impulsive, finite-duration and stochastic inputs into node-resolved response timescales. Here, we develop a theory for network dynamics near stable operating states that answers this question. The framework identifies a canonical set of gains and timescales shared across deterministic and stochastic forcing and expresses them through matrix resolvents, spectra and directed walks. In positive, sufficiently damped networks, the walk representation gives a simple physical picture: response strength accumulates multiplicatively along a single path, whereas response time accumulates additively, through local intrinsic time constants. Competing pathways, feedback and inhibition further reshape propagation by amplifying, suppressing, reversing or delaying signals. We derive perturbative criteria that specify when these signatures, and the resulting node rankings, persist beyond the positive regime. Applied to a Wilson--Cowan model of the primate cortex, the theory links structural connectivity, excitatory--inhibitory balance and local biophysical timescales to hierarchical response timescales. Our results provide a mechanistic framework for input-dependent timescales in finite heterogeneous networks.

item.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Chengqian Ma, Yuanze Zeng, Hongyu Wang, Mingfeng Lin, YiCheng Xiao, Yu Chen, Pengyu Li, WenHao Wang, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
arXiv:2611.23153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

item.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan
arXiv:2611.22132v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).

item.title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Cheston Tan, Bihan Wen, Yeying Jin
arXiv:2610.40339v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 805 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured proxies to condition video generation. Our agentic framework explicitly tracks and updates game states to support character-aware adaptive masking and world-anchored spatial conditioning, improving character identity preservation and spatial consistency. Experiments on WBench show that our method achieves higher gameplay fidelity with comparable video quality and spatiotemporal consistency, while using fewer parameters and less training data than state-of-the-art world models. These advantages are also retained in our two-step real-time variant. Overall, Wizard combines agentic control with structured proxy-based generation to enable player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

item.title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mehul Arora, Dhruv Agarwal, Ambuj Agrawal
arXiv:2611.22395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.

item.title: CutAgent: Creative-Gene-Driven Planning and Experience-Guided Self-Refinement for High-CTR E-commerce Advertising Video Creation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xuyue Huang, Guanbo Huang, Jiasong Feng, Run Ling, Ao Ma, Xi Zhao, Yaoyu Li, Jie Gao, Ke Cao, Wei Feng, Zhanjie Zhang, Hao Wang, Jinghe Hu
arXiv:2611.22418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: E-commerce advertising video creation requires both high-level creative planning and reliable multi-modal production. However, existing methods often map product attributes directly to scripts or editing decisions without explicitly modeling advertising strategies, narrative structures, and production styles. They also have limited ability to reuse past production failures. To address these limitations, we propose $\textbf{CutAgent}$, a dual-agent framework that formulates advertising video creation as a Plan--Execute--Self-Evolve process. CutAgent comprises two collaborative agents, $\textbf{GeneAgent}$ and $\textbf{VideoAgent}$, connected by a structured creative gene that bridges product understanding and video production. GeneAgent maps multi-modal product inputs---textual attributes together with product images---to creative genes that specify narrative units and production rules. To train GeneAgent, we construct $\textbf{CutAgent-70K}$ with approximately 70K samples of product attributes/images, reverse-extracted creative genes, cleaned clip pools, and real-world CTR, and apply high-CTR supervised fine-tuning followed by CTR-guided GRPO. Guided by the generated gene, VideoAgent retrieves category-then-gene failure--correction experiences from a long-term memory as constraints for shot-script planning, then coordinates material retrieval, narration, subtitles, music, and timeline rendering. Independently, a reflection loop diagnoses quality defects, revises deficient production decisions, and writes verified corrections back to memory for later retrieval. Experiments on $\textbf{CutAgent-Eval}$ show that CutAgent outperforms representative baselines in e-commerce advertising video creation, achieving the highest online CTR of $\textbf{2.21\%}$.

item.title: AerialOcc: Unified 3D Aerial Perception without Task-Specific Head
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Fan Liu, Xiang Gu, Baoyu Lv, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuye Ma, Yuhui Zheng
arXiv:2611.18770v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at https://github.com/guxiang2002/AerialOcc

item.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
arXiv:2611.23211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

item.title: GaussianMamba: Geometric and Relational State Space Scanning of 3D Gaussian Primitives
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
A. Enes Doruk, Ozgur Erkent
arXiv:2611.22742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction requires representing complex spatial structures and modeling contextual relationships across a scene. 3D Gaussian primitives provide a sparse and adaptive representation of scene geometry and semantics, while Mamba offers efficient sequence modeling for capturing dependencies among primitives. However, Gaussian primitives are irregular and unordered, making sequence construction challenging, as conventional spatial ordering may overlook their anisotropic geometry and feature-semantic relationships. In this paper, we present GaussianMamba, a dual-branch Mamba framework that explicitly incorporates Gaussian-specific geometric and feature-semantic relationships into complementary scanning strategies. The first branch refines a locality-preserving traversal using anisotropic Gaussian support derived from primitive scale and orientation. The second branch reorders spatially organized groups according to feature-semantic affinity and adjusts local features using geometry-weighted semantic differences. The resulting sequences are processed by separate Mamba modules, and their features are fused through a support-aware mechanism that incorporates local feature discrepancies arising from the distinct scanning paths. Experiments on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360 demonstrate consistent improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 in both IoU and mIoU.

item.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Javad Amirian, Armin Kiani, Lo\"ic Schaeffer, Tim Sprecher, Mohamed Taha, Karthik Yadati
arXiv:2611.21938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. item.title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou, Dengyang Jiang, Zeyue Tian, Xuanhua He, Ryan Xu, Yunyang Ge, Sihui Ji, Yunlong Lin, Kaihang Pan, Hongru Yan, Sixiang Chen, Dianyi Wang, Julian Zhang, Weijie Kong, Changlin Li, Lanqing Guo, Zhao Zhong, Qifeng Chen, Harry Yang
arXiv:2611.06518v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

item.title: Kolibri: Color Finds the Place, Refinement Sets the Pose for RGB-D Localization in Colored Point Clouds
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Leonel Aguilar, Bartu Tuncay, Christoph Hoelscher
arXiv:2611.22829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5{\deg}) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.

item.description:

arXiv:2609.17953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can produce Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) that sound plausible yet remain inconsistent with the visual evidence they cite. We present Explanation-Driven Counterfactual Testing (EDCT), an intervention-based protocol that extracts visual concepts cited in a model's explanation, applies verified minimal edits to them, and tests whether the resulting answer and explanation remain consistent with the edited image. Using this protocol, we create EDCT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning three complementary domains: knowledge-intensive visual question answering (OK-VQA), safety-critical driving (DriveLM), and 3D spatial reasoning (3DSRBench). Across the evaluated VLMs, EDCT reveals substantial faithfulness gaps, with models frequently producing responses inconsistent with verified visual changes. Finally, our fine-tuning study suggests that EDCT-generated counterfactuals provide high-impact training signals.
